lesson.title: Introdução a Rede Neural
lesson.description: Este encontro tem por objetivo apresentar as Redes Neurais para as pessoas desenvolvedoras. A sua concepção, aplicação, algoritmos de treinamento e evolução serão abordadas. Com o término da instrução, espera-se que as pessoas desenvolvedoras possam estar mais familiarizadas com a forma como as Redes Neurais são desenvolvidas.
related_labels: Paradigmas e modelos de desenvolvimento de sistemas de informação

before_phase4_candidates.label: McCulloch-Pitts neuron model
before_phase4_candidates.description: The first computational model of a neuron, proposed by Warren McCulloch and Walter Pitts in 1943, representing neurons as simple electrical circuits.
coverage_criteria: Identify McCulloch and Pitts as the authors of the first neuron model in 1943.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The video clearly states that the first step towards neural networks was in 1943 when McCulloch and Pitts wrote a paper on how neurons might work and modeled a simple neural network with electrical circuits.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This candidate captures a single historical milestone without combining with later developments, making it checkable with a single identification question.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Hebbian learning
before_phase4_candidates.description: The principle that neural pathways are strengthened each time they are used, introduced by Donald Hebb in his 1949 book 'The Organization of Behavior'.
coverage_criteria: State that Hebbian learning means neural pathways strengthen with use.
before_phase4_candidates.source_name: Breve história das redes neurais

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The video mentions Hebb's book and the key idea that neural pathways are strengthened each time they are used.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Rosenblatt's Perceptron
before_phase4_candidates.description: A single-layer neural network model that computes a weighted sum of inputs, subtracts a threshold, and outputs one of two classes; built in hardware and the oldest neural network still in use.
coverage_criteria: Explain how the perceptron performs binary classification using weighted sum and threshold.
Identify Rosenblatt as the creator of the perceptron in 1958.
before_phase4_candidates.source_name: Breve história das redes neurais

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The video provides a detailed description of the perceptron: it computes a weighted sum, subtracts a threshold, and outputs one of two values; it is the oldest NN still in use.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: The perceptron is a core concept in neural networks, and focusing on its mechanism (weighted sum, threshold, binary output) allows assessment of fundamental understanding without overcomplicating with later variants.

before_phase4_candidates.label: ADALINE and MADALINE
before_phase4_candidates.description: Early adaptive linear neural network models (Multiple Adaptive Linear Elements) developed by Bernard Widrow and Marcian Hoff; MADALINE was the first neural network applied to a real-world problem (echo cancellation) and remains in commercial use.
coverage_criteria: Name ADALINE and MADALINE as early neural networks that used adaptive linear elements.
Identify echo cancellation as the real-world application of MADALINE.
before_phase4_candidates.source_name: Breve história das redes neurais

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The source explicitly states that ADALINE and MADALINE were named for their use of multiple adaptive linear elements, that MADALINE was the first applied to a real-world problem, and that it is still in commercial use for eliminating echoes on phone lines.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This candidate highlights an important step toward practical neural networks, distinct from the perceptron, and can be checked by asking about the name expansion and application.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Minsky & Papert critique and AI winter
before_phase4_candidates.description: The 1969 book 'Perceptrons' by Marvin Minsky and Seymour Papert proved the limitations of perceptrons, leading to a halt in neural network funding and research until 1981.
coverage_criteria: Explain that Minsky and Papert's work demonstrated limitations of perceptrons, causing a decline in neural network research.

extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: Activation functions are critical components; ReLU is a widely used choice and the source explicitly discusses its advantages and demonstrates its usage.

reconciled_candidates.label: Perceptron
reconciled_candidates.description: The perceptron is a single-layer neural network that performs binary classification by computing a weighted sum of inputs, adding a bias, and applying a threshold (step) activation function. Introduced by Frank Rosenblatt in 1958.
coverage_criteria: Explain how the perceptron computes output from inputs using weights, bias, and step function.
Identify Rosenblatt as the creator and 1958 as the year.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: These candidates all describe the perceptron model: its architecture, computation, and binary classification. They are near-duplicates and are merged into one cohesive concept.

reconciled_candidates.label: McCulloch-Pitts neuron model
reconciled_candidates.description: The first computational model of a neuron, proposed by Warren McCulloch and Walter Pitts in 1943, representing neurons as simple electrical circuits.
coverage_criteria: Identify McCulloch and Pitts as the authors of the first neuron model in 1943.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: This candidate stands alone as a distinct historical milestone in neural network development.

reconciled_candidates.label: Hebbian learning
reconciled_candidates.description: The principle that neural pathways are strengthened each time they are used, introduced by Donald Hebb in his 1949 book 'The Organization of Behavior'.
coverage_criteria: State that Hebbian learning means neural pathways strengthen with use.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: This candidate stands alone as a distinct historical milestone in neural network development.

reconciled_candidates.label: ADALINE and MADALINE
reconciled_candidates.description: Early adaptive linear neural network models (Multiple Adaptive Linear Elements) developed by Bernard Widrow and Marcian Hoff; MADALINE was the first neural network applied to a real-world problem (echo cancellation) and remains in commercial use.
coverage_criteria: Name ADALINE and MADALINE as early neural networks that used adaptive linear elements.
Identify echo cancellation as the real-world application of MADALINE.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: This candidate stands alone as a distinct historical milestone in neural network development.

reconciled_candidates.label: Minsky & Papert critique and AI winter
reconciled_candidates.description: The 1969 book 'Perceptrons' by Marvin Minsky and Seymour Papert proved the limitations of perceptrons, leading to a halt in neural network funding and research until 1981.
coverage_criteria: Explain that Minsky and Papert's work demonstrated limitations of perceptrons, causing a decline in neural network research.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: This candidate stands alone as a distinct historical turning point in neural network development.

reconciled_candidates.label: Hopfield networks and the revival of neural network research
reconciled_candidates.description: John Hopfield's 1982 paper to the National Academy of Sciences, combined with the US-Japan Conference on Cooperative Competitive Neural Networks, rekindled interest and funding in neural networks after the AI winter.
coverage_criteria: State that Hopfield's 1982 approach and the US-Japan conference helped restart neural network funding.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: This candidate stands alone as a distinct historical milestone in neural network development.

reconciled_candidates.label: Feedforward Neural Network
reconciled_candidates.description: A feedforward neural network is organized in layers where connections flow only from input to output without cycles. Forward propagation computes outputs by sequentially applying weights, biases, and activation functions through the layers.
coverage_criteria: Describe the architecture of a feedforward network (input, hidden, output layers).
Explain the forward propagation process for a simple network.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: These candidates cover feedforward architecture, neuron layering, and forward propagation, together forming a complete concept of feedforward network operation.

reconciled_candidates.label: Activation Functions
reconciled_candidates.description: Activation functions introduce non-linearity into neural networks, enabling them to learn complex patterns. Common functions include sigmoid, tanh, ReLU, and step, each with specific properties and output ranges.
coverage_criteria: List at least three activation functions and their typical use cases.
Explain why non-linear activation functions are necessary in hidden layers.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: These candidates describe common activation functions (sigmoid, tanh, ReLU, step) and their purpose; they are merged to provide a comprehensive overview of activation functions.

reconciled_candidates.label: Backpropagation
reconciled_candidates.description: Backpropagation is the primary algorithm for training neural networks. It computes gradients of the loss function with respect to weights using the chain rule, propagating errors backward from output to input, and updates weights to minimize loss.
coverage_criteria: Explain the steps of backpropagation: forward pass, loss calculation, backward pass, weight update.
Describe the role of the chain rule in computing gradients.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: These candidates all explain the backpropagation algorithm for training neural networks, using chain rule to compute gradients; they are near-duplicates.

reconciled_candidates.label: Gradient Descent Optimization
reconciled_candidates.description: Gradient descent is an iterative optimization algorithm used to train neural networks by minimizing a loss function. Parameters are updated by subtracting the product of the learning rate and the gradient. Key aspects include learning rate, epochs, and variants like Adam.
coverage_criteria: Write the gradient descent update rule and explain the role of the learning rate.
Define an epoch and describe how the number of epochs affects training.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: These candidates cover gradient descent optimization, including learning rate, epochs, update rules, and the perceptron training loop; together they teach the core optimization concept.

reconciled_candidates.label: Recurrent Neural Network (RNN)
reconciled_candidates.description: A recurrent neural network has feedback connections that allow it to maintain a memory state, making it suitable for sequential data processing. Unlike feedforward networks, RNNs can process sequences by reusing activations across time steps.
coverage_criteria: Explain how RNNs differ from feedforward networks due to recurrent loops.
Identify an application domain where RNNs are preferred.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: This candidate provides a standalone description of recurrent neural network architecture.

reconciled_candidates.label: Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM)
reconciled_candidates.description: LSTM is a specialized recurrent neural network that uses gated memory cells (input, forget, output gates) to learn long-term dependencies and mitigate the vanishing gradient problem. Proposed in 1997 by Hochreiter and Schmidhuber.
coverage_criteria: Describe the purpose of the forget, input, and output gates in an LSTM cell.
Compare LSTM with a simple RNN in terms of handling long sequences.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: These candidates describe LSTM architecture, including gates and historical context; they are merged into a single LSTM concept.

reconciled_candidates.label: Convolutional Neural Network (CNN)
reconciled_candidates.description: A deep learning architecture designed for grid-structured data, using convolutional layers to learn spatial hierarchies of features, pooling layers for dimensionality reduction, and fully-connected layers for classification. Influenced by Yann LeCun's 1998 paper on gradient-based learning for document recognition.
coverage_criteria: Describe the operations of a convolutional layer (kernel, stride, feature map).
Explain the role of pooling layers and how output size depends on input size, filter size, and padding.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: These candidates explain convolutional neural networks, including architecture, layer output size, and a key historical paper; they form a unified CNN concept.

reconciled_candidates.label: Loss Functions
reconciled_candidates.description: Loss functions quantify the error between predictions and true values during training. Mean squared error is used for regression, binary cross-entropy for binary classification, and categorical cross-entropy for multi-class classification.
coverage_criteria: Match loss functions (MSE, binary crossentropy, categorical crossentropy) to problem types.
Explain why cross-entropy is preferred over MSE for classification.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: These candidates cover loss functions for neural networks; they are merged to cover common loss types.

reconciled_candidates.label: Overfitting and Dropout Regularization
reconciled_candidates.description: Overfitting occurs when a model memorizes training data noise, resulting in poor generalization. Dropout is a regularization technique that randomly drops neurons during training to prevent overfitting.
coverage_criteria: Define overfitting and underfitting, and suggest at least one technique to combat overfitting.
Explain how dropout works during training and state the typical range for the drop probability.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: These candidates describe overfitting and dropout as a regularization technique; they are merged to teach model generalization.

reconciled_candidates.label: Neural Network Taxonomy Chart
reconciled_candidates.description: An overview chart presenting a wide variety of neural network architectures, including feedforward, recurrent, convolutional, and generative models, along with their components.
coverage_criteria: Name and briefly describe at least three distinct architectures shown in the chart.
Identify the arrow-based notation used to differentiate network types.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: This single candidate provides an overview chart of neural network architectures.

reconciled_candidates.label: Autoencoder
reconciled_candidates.description: An unsupervised neural network that encodes input into a compressed representation and then decodes it back to reconstruct the original input, used for dimensionality reduction and feature learning.
coverage_criteria: Sketch the general structure of an autoencoder (encoder, bottleneck, decoder).
Explain how an autoencoder can be used for data compression.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: This single candidate describes autoencoder architecture and purpose.

reconciled_candidates.label: Generative Adversarial Network (GAN)
reconciled_candidates.description: A generative model framework where two networks, a generator and a discriminator, compete: the generator creates synthetic data, and the discriminator evaluates authenticity, improving both through adversarial training.
coverage_criteria: Describe the roles of generator and discriminator.
Explain the adversarial training process in simple terms.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: Standalone concept covering the core GAN idea.

reconciled_candidates.label: Hebbian Learning Rule
reconciled_candidates.description: Based on Hebb's postulate ('neurons that fire together wire together'), this learning rule strengthens connections between co-active neurons, providing a biological inspiration for early neural network learning algorithms.
coverage_criteria: State Hebb's postulate.
Describe one Hebbian learning rule variation.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: Standalone concept on biologically inspired learning.

reconciled_candidates.label: Deep Residual Network (DRN)
reconciled_candidates.description: An advanced architecture using skip connections (residual blocks) that allow gradients to pass directly through very deep networks, enabling training of networks with hundreds of layers without degradation.
coverage_criteria: Explain what a residual block is.
Mention a benefit of skip connections for deep networks.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: Standalone concept introducing residual connections.

reconciled_candidates.label: TensorFlow and Keras Frameworks
reconciled_candidates.description: TensorFlow is an open-source library for numerical computation and machine learning; Keras is a high-level API built on top that simplifies defining, training, and evaluating neural network models. Together they provide a productive environment for deep learning.
coverage_criteria: Describe the relationship between TensorFlow and Keras.
Write a minimal Keras Sequential model definition.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: Two candidates covering TensorFlow+Keras and Keras alone are merged into a single framework concept; the Keras-only candidate is represented within this broader description.

reconciled_candidates.label: Linear Algebra Foundations for Neural Networks
reconciled_candidates.description: Neural network computations rely on linear algebra concepts: vector spaces, inner products (dot products), norms, and linear transformations, which underlie neuron operations and weight calculations.
coverage_criteria: Define a linear vector space and list key axioms.
Compute the dot product of two vectors.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: Standalone foundational mathematical concept.

reconciled_candidates.label: Neural Network Training Process
reconciled_candidates.description: Training a neural network involves iterating over the dataset for several epochs. Each epoch consists of forward propagation (computing predictions and storing cached values), cost computation, backpropagation (gradient calculation using cached values), and parameter updates. Proper parameter initialization (small random weights, zero biases) is essential to break symmetry and enable learning.
coverage_criteria: List the steps in one training iteration.
Explain why random weight initialization is needed.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: Parameter initialization and forward-propagation caching are integral parts of the overall training process; they are combined into a single concept covering the full training loop.

reconciled_candidates.label: Input Encoding for Neural Networks
reconciled_candidates.description: Non-vector data must be encoded into numerical vectors before feeding neural networks. Common strategies include binary encoding for integers and one-hot encoding for categorical output classes, as demonstrated in the Fizz Buzz example.
coverage_criteria: Propose a vector representation for a simple non-numeric input.
Explain the difference between binary encoding and one-hot encoding.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: Standalone practical skill for data preparation.

reconciled_candidates.label: Neural Network Architecture and Parameter Shapes
reconciled_candidates.description: Neural networks consist of an input layer, one or more hidden layers, and an output layer. Each neuron computes a linear combination of inputs plus a bias (z = w^T x + b). The layer_dims list specifies the number of neurons per layer and determines parameter shapes: weight matrix W has shape (current layer, previous layer), and bias vector b has shape (current layer, 1).
coverage_criteria: Describe the three types of layers in a neural network.
Given a layer_dims list, determine the shape of W for a specific layer.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: High-level architecture and implementation-level parameter shapes are merged into one concept covering both the structure and its computational consequences.

reconciled_candidates.label: Perceptron Limitation and Linear Separability
reconciled_candidates.description: A single perceptron can only solve linearly separable problems—datasets where a straight line (or hyperplane) can perfectly separate the classes. Non-linearly separable problems, such as XOR, require multi-layer networks to create complex decision boundaries.
coverage_criteria: Identify whether a simple 2D dataset is linearly separable.
Explain why a single perceptron fails on XOR.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: Linear separability and perceptron limitation are taught together as the motivation for deeper architectures.

reconciled_candidates.label: Solving XOR with a Multi-Layer Neural Network
reconciled_candidates.description: The XOR problem can be solved by a feedforward network with a hidden layer that computes intermediate features (e.g., AND, OR) and an output layer that combines them, demonstrating how hidden layers create non-linear decision boundaries.
coverage_criteria: Describe the architecture used to solve XOR.
Explain the role of the hidden layer in the XOR solution.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: Standalone example applying multi-layer networks to a classic problem.

reconciled_candidates.label: Fizz Buzz Neural Network Example
reconciled_candidates.description: The Fizz Buzz problem can be treated as a classification task by binary-encoding input numbers and one-hot encoding the four possible outputs, then training a neural network with 10 inputs, 25 hidden units, and 4 outputs to learn the pattern.
coverage_criteria: Explain how the Fizz Buzz problem is converted to a classification task.
Describe the input and output encodings used in the example.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: Standalone end-to-end application illustration.

reconciled_candidates.label: Model Evaluation: Train/Test Split and Accuracy
reconciled_candidates.description: Evaluating a model requires splitting data into a training set (to learn parameters) and a test set (to assess generalization). Accuracy measures the proportion of correct predictions, providing a simple performance metric.
coverage_criteria: Implement a train/test split on a given dataset.
Calculate accuracy from predicted and true labels.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: Train/test split and accuracy are complementary evaluation concepts merged into a single lesson-local idea about model assessment.

reconciled_candidates.label: Manual Perceptron Implementation vs. Scikit-learn
reconciled_candidates.description: Implementing a perceptron from scratch (manually coding weight updates) highlights core mechanics; using scikit-learn's Perceptron class simplifies the process with pre-built functions, illustrating the productivity gains of high-level libraries.
coverage_criteria: List the key steps in a manual perceptron implementation.
Identify the scikit-learn classes and functions that replace manual code.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: Standalone comparative concept reinforcing library advantages.

reconciled_candidates.label: Bias in neural networks
reconciled_candidates.description: The bias term is a constant added to the weighted sum of inputs, allowing the decision boundary to shift from the origin. It is often implemented as weight w0 with a fixed input of -1.
coverage_criteria: The student can identify the role of bias in enabling the decision boundary to not pass through the origin.
The student can explain how the bias is implemented in code (input -1 with weight w0) when calculating the weighted sum.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: This candidate stands alone as a specific, teachable component of the perceptron model.

reconciled_candidates.label: Dataset preparation for neural networks
reconciled_candidates.description: Datasets for neural networks consist of features and a target variable. Data must be numeric, and categorical variables need encoding. Common sources include Kaggle and the UCI repository.
coverage_criteria: The student can examine a CSV file and identify which columns are features and which is the target.
The student can suggest transformations to convert categorical data to numerical format for use in neural networks.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: This candidate stands alone as a distinct data preparation concept.

reconciled_candidates.label: Multilayer Perceptron (MLP)
reconciled_candidates.description: An extension of the simple perceptron with one or more hidden layers, enabling it to solve non-linearly separable problems at increased computational cost.
coverage_criteria: The student can differentiate a simple perceptron from a multilayer perceptron in a diagram by the presence of hidden layers.
The student can justify why a multilayer perceptron is necessary for datasets that are not linearly separable.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: This candidate stands alone as an architectural concept.

reconciled_candidates.label: Artificial Neural Network definition
reconciled_candidates.description: An artificial neural network is a predictive model inspired by the brain, composed of interconnected neurons that perform weighted computations and produce an output via an activation function.
coverage_criteria: The student can define an artificial neural network and describe its basic components (neurons, connections, activation function).
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: This candidate stands alone as a foundational introduction.

reconciled_candidates.label: Defining a Keras Sequential model
reconciled_candidates.description: A Keras Sequential model is defined by stacking layers linearly. It involves creating a Sequential object, adding Dense (fully connected) layers with a specified number of neurons and activation function, and setting the input shape for the first layer.
coverage_criteria: The student can write code to create a Sequential model and add at least one Dense layer, correctly specifying the input_shape argument (matching the number of features) and a valid activation function.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: These three candidates describe tightly coupled steps in constructing a Keras Sequential model: creating the Sequential object, adding Dense layers, and specifying input dimensions. They form a single, coherent concept about model definition.
